# Diagnosing Fuel Flow Issues: The "Reserve Only" Symptom

When a motorcycle engine cranks and fires up exclusively when the fuel petcock is set to reserve, but remains dead in the ON position, you are dealing with a classic volumetric flow restriction or an air leak within the low-pressure fuel system. This isn't an electrical mystery; the ECU or ignition coil is functioning correctly because it receives spark immediately once fuel reaches the carburetor injectors or fuel rail. The root cause lies entirely in how the liquid gets from the tank to the intake manifold.

## Understanding the Petcock Architecture

To troubleshoot this effectively, you must understand that a standard three-position petcockâON, RES, and OFFâoperates via two distinct valves. In the ON position, the primary valve opens fully, allowing fuel to flow directly from the main chamber of the tank into the line. The reserve valve remains closed during this phase. When you switch to RES, the primary valve closes mechanically, and a secondary valve opens to draw fuel from a lower chamber or a dedicated reserve port in the tank.

If your bike runs only in RES, the diagnosis usually points to one of three specific failure modes: the primary valve is partially obstructed, the main supply line is restricted, or there is an air leak at the junction where the petcock meets the fuel rail.

## The Most Common Culprit: Clogged Main Jet Filter

In carbureted engines, the most frequent cause for this behavior is a clogged mesh filter located inside the petcock body itself. Over time, sediment, rust flakes, or debris settles at the bottom of the tank. When you turn the petcock to ON, fuel flows over this primary screen. If the screen is blocked by particulate matter, the flow rate drops significantly below what the engine requires for idle and low-RPM operation.

However, when you switch to RES, the fuel line connects to a different port, often located higher up in the tank or bypassing the main sediment trap entirely. This provides a cleaner path with sufficient volume to keep the engine running.

**Implementation Check:**
Before disassembling the petcock, perform a visual inspection of the fuel tank interior if accessible. Look for dark sludge accumulation at the bottom. If the tank has never been cleaned or drained recently, the likelihood of sediment buildup causing a restriction in the primary line is high.

Disassemble the petcock carefully. You will typically find a fine mesh screen on the outlet side of the ON valve. Remove this filter and inspect it under good lighting. If it appears clogged with black gunk, clean it with a solvent like brake cleaner or acetone, then reinstall it with fresh fuel. Often, a simple cleaning restores normal flow in the ON position.

## Secondary Causes: Restriction and Air Leaks

If the mesh filter is clean, the issue may be a restriction further down the line. Inspect the rubber fuel hose connecting the petcock to the carburetor or fuel pump. Look for internal collapse, kinks, or partial blockage caused by age-hardening of the rubber. A restricted hose acts as a throttle, limiting the flow rate required for the ON setting while the reserve position might draw from a slightly different source or have less resistance in that specific branch.

Another critical failure point is an air leak at the petcock outlet seal. Modern fuel systems rely on a vacuum seal to prevent air from being sucked into the intake manifold when the primary valve closes (even momentarily during throttle changes) or simply to maintain consistent pressure. If the O-ring sealing the petcock output is dried out, cracked, or misaligned, air can enter the system in the ON position, creating an air-fuel mixture that is too lean for combustion at idle.

In the RES position, the flow dynamics change, sometimes masking a minor leak long enough to start the engine, though this is less reliable. If you suspect an air leak, replace the petcock output O-ring with a new one of the exact same cross-sectional dimension. Do not use generic seals from a general hardware store; automotive fuel system tolerances are tight.

## When to Replace the Petcock

Sometimes cleaning and resealing isn't enough. Internal valve stems can warp or develop micro-cracks that prevent them from seating fully in the ON position. If you have cleaned the filter, replaced the O-ring, ensured the tank is free of debris, and the bike still refuses to start on ON, the petcock body itself likely requires replacement.

There are no complex diagnostic commands or code snippets for fuel flow; this is purely a mechanical hardware diagnosis. However, if your motorcycle uses an electric fuel pump integrated with the petcock assembly, ensure you are checking the primary filter screen *inside* the tank as well, not just at the petcock outlet. A clogged in-tank filter on the pump side will manifest similarly, starving the engine regardless of the petcock position.

Addressing this issue promptly prevents running out of fuel unexpectedly and avoids damaging the carburetor jets or fuel injectors with debris stirred up by restricted flow.
